lesson.title: When the Supreme Court Got It Wrong
lesson.summary: In Korematsu v. United States, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of Japanese American internment in 1944, a ruling now almost universally condemned as one of the Court's gravest errors.
lesson.body:
The internment described in the previous chapter did not go entirely unchallenged. Fred Korematsu, a young Japanese American man living in California, refused to comply with the government's removal order and was arrested and convicted for violating it. His case worked its way up to the United States Supreme Court, which had the power of judicial review, the authority established generations earlier to determine whether government actions were consistent with the Constitution.

In December 1944, the Supreme Court ruled against Korematsu by a vote of six to three, upholding the constitutionality of the exclusion order. Writing for the majority, Justice Hugo Black reasoned that the exclusion was justified by 'pressing public necessity,' accepting the military's claims about the danger of sabotage and espionage without meaningfully questioning whether those claims were true. The Court did state that racial discrimination by the government deserved especially close scrutiny, an idea that later became an important legal principle, but it still allowed the internment to stand.

The dissenting justices saw the case far more clearly. Justice Frank Murphy called the ruling a 'legalization of racism,' arguing that the exclusion order rested on unproven assumptions about an entire group of people based solely on ancestry. Justice Robert Jackson warned that the decision set a dangerous precedent, comparing an unconstitutional order upheld by the Court to a loaded weapon left available for any future official who might want to use race as a justification for depriving citizens of their rights.

History has vindicated the dissenters rather than the majority. In 1983, a federal court in California vacated Korematsu's original conviction after researchers discovered that government lawyers had withheld and altered evidence showing military officials knew Japanese Americans posed no actual security threat when they argued the case before the Supreme Court. That ruling corrected Korematsu's personal record, but it did not erase the Supreme Court's 1944 decision itself, which technically remained on the books as precedent for decades. It was not until 2018, in an unrelated case, that the Supreme Court publicly repudiated Korematsu, with the Chief Justice writing that the decision had been 'gravely wrong the day it was decided.' Korematsu v. United States is remembered today less as a guide to how courts should rule than as a warning about how fear and prejudice can lead even the nation's highest court to fail in its duty to protect constitutional rights.
